drafts.headline: Interest income is a balance times a rate, and holding it flat cannot track either.
drafts.plain: A company that builds a cash pile into rising deposit rates earns dramatically more interest, and a company that spends one earns less. Carrying last year's figure forward misses both moves at once. Drive it off the cash balance at the deposit rate, the same way the rest of the book does.
drafts.evidence: Bias -1.641 log (about 5.2 times too low), average miss 2.177, wrong in the same direction in 76% of cases, and the sign holds across every bootstrap block tested (n=25).
drafts.why_scope: ALL. It is arithmetic about how the line is generated, not a fact about any one company.
drafts.overturned_by: Nothing. This is arithmetic.

drafts.headline: Price export forecasts run about 51% too low for ARCC.
drafts.plain: The method misses this driver in the same direction almost every time, not at random. That is a fixable defect rather than noise — find what is wired wrong before adding any correction factor.
drafts.evidence: Bias -0.411 log (about 51% too low), average miss 0.474, wrong in the same direction in 76% of cases, and the sign holds across every bootstrap block tested (n=25).
drafts.why_scope: A robust bias in one driver may be this company's disclosure, its whole class's economics, or our method. Decide which before filing.
drafts.overturned_by: A later run of the same name where the sign no longer holds across bootstrap blocks.
drafts.declined: Part of ONE finding about the inflation path rather than several about several drivers: local price, raw materials per tonne, overheads per tonne and G&A are all under-forecast because the origin's last published inflation understated what Egypt ran. Correcting any one of them alone would manufacture a margin, which is the lesson already registered on gross profit. Held as watch flags.

drafts.headline: Haulage cost follows the EXPORT tonne, so a cost per tonne despatched misprices it.
drafts.plain: Cement sold at home moves a short distance to a local customer; clinker sold abroad moves to a port. Spreading haulage across every tonne despatched makes the cost look like a rate that inflation moves, when it is really a mix effect. When the export share falls, a per-despatched-tonne driver overstates the cost.
drafts.evidence: Bias -0.693 log (about 2.0 times too low), average miss 0.791, wrong in the same direction in 76% of cases, and the sign holds across every bootstrap block tested (n=25).
drafts.why_scope: CLASS. It is about a producer with a bulk export leg and a domestic leg, which is the shape of this class, not something peculiar to one company.
drafts.overturned_by: A producer whose local and export haulage rates per tonne are disclosed and turn out to be the same.

drafts.headline: An exogenous volume anchor has to be scored against 'no change' before it is trusted.
drafts.plain: The protocol asks for volume to be driven by something outside the company — population, credit, activity — rather than by its own trend. That is the right instinct and it is not self-validating: the anchor can point the wrong way. Score it against simply carrying last year's volume forward, and if it loses, the driver is mis-specified and no correction factor will repair it.
drafts.evidence: Negative skill against the freeze benchmark at horizons 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, worst -0.260.
drafts.why_scope: ALL. This is a rule about how to check a driver, not a finding about cement or about Egypt. Any study that anchors volume on an exogenous series can run the same test in one line.
drafts.overturned_by: A study where the exogenous anchor loses to freeze and the anchor is still the better forecast out of sample.

drafts.headline: If perfect knowledge of the macro path makes a MARGIN forecast worse, the two legs were cancelling.
drafts.plain: A margin is a difference, so its error is the difference of two errors. When revenue and cost are both wrong in the same direction the margin can come out nearly right for the wrong reason. Handing the model the true inflation and currency path repairs the two legs by different amounts and breaks that cancellation — which is why the margin forecast can get WORSE with better information. The practical consequence is the important part: never recalibrate one leg onto a fresh actual without recalibrating the other on the same one.
drafts.evidence: Average miss 1.265 as known, 1.339 with perfect foresight of inflation — the macro share is only -5.8%.
drafts.why_scope: ALL. It follows from a margin being a difference, which is true of every company. It is also the mechanism behind the escalator rule already in the register, seen from the other end.
drafts.overturned_by: A run where the macro split is positive on the margin and negative on both of the legs that make it, which would mean the cancellation runs the other way.

drafts.headline: The interest income error is the company, not the currency.
drafts.plain: Re-running every forecast with perfect foresight of inflation barely improves it. So devaluation is not the explanation, and looking for a macro fix would waste the effort.
drafts.evidence: Average miss 2.177 as known, 2.177 with perfect foresight of inflation — the macro share is only 0.0%.
drafts.why_scope: Almost always ALL — 'check whether the macro explains it before assuming it does' is a method rule — but the specific finding may be about this market.
drafts.overturned_by: A market or period where the same decomposition puts most of the error on the macro path.
drafts.declined: The same finding restated per driver. It is registered once, on gross profit, where the macro share is actually NEGATIVE and the mechanism is visible; the others are the arithmetic consequence of it and filing them separately would inflate the register without adding evidence.

drafts.headline: The amort bias changes direction between regimes.
drafts.plain: It runs one way in one period and the other way in the next. Averaging them produces a correction that is wrong in both. Record it, do not correct for it.
drafts.evidence: By era: E1 pre-2022 +0.348; E2 devaluation sequence +0.000.
drafts.why_scope: A sign that flips with the regime is usually about the market or the period, not the company — but say which.
drafts.overturned_by: A longer record in which one sign dominates across all regimes.
drafts.declined: Registered once, on profit after tax, which is the line the instability actually matters for. The others (amortisation, other income, majority profit) either flip on a contractual schedule or are the same series under another name.

drafts.headline: A bottom-line bias that flips sign between regimes is instability, and must not be corrected.
drafts.plain: Net profit is what is left after everything else, so it inherits every driver's error and the currency's on top. When its miss runs one way before a devaluation sequence and the other way through it, the average is a number that was true in neither period. Report the instability; do not correct for it.
drafts.evidence: By era: E1 pre-2022 -0.581; E2 devaluation sequence +0.006.
drafts.why_scope: ALL. It is the general rule about era-flipping biases, applied where it bites hardest — the most levered line in the statement.
drafts.overturned_by: A record long enough that one sign dominates the bottom line across every regime it contains.

drafts.headline: A correction to price export worked and must still be checked against the rest of the book.
drafts.plain: A fudge factor that improves this one name can be hiding a defect in how we set the model up. Before adopting it, check it matches how that driver is built everywhere else.
drafts.evidence: Applied +0.023 at origin FY2021; average miss changed -0.023.
drafts.why_scope: If the correction turns out to be fixing our own mis-specification, the lesson is ALL and is about specification. If the company is genuinely unusual, it is STOCK.
drafts.overturned_by: Evidence that the driver is built the same way across the book and this name still needs the correction.
drafts.declined: The candidate failed one or both clauses of the correction test and is a watch flag. The transferable lesson — that a correction which degrades out of sample is a specification defect — is registered once rather than once per driver.

drafts.headline: A correction that makes the out-of-sample error WORSE is a specification defect, not a bias.
drafts.plain: It is tempting to treat any consistent miss as something a multiplier can fix. Test the multiplier the way you would test a forecast: estimate it only on data that had already resolved, then apply it forward. If the error gets worse, the problem is in how the driver is wired, and a correction would only hide it.
drafts.evidence: Applied -0.108 at origin FY2022; average miss changed -0.108.
drafts.why_scope: ALL. It is a rule about how a correction is tested, and the test is the same whatever the driver or the company.
drafts.overturned_by: A driver whose correction degrades out of sample and is nevertheless shown to be a calibration problem rather than a specification one.

drafts.plain: A fudge factor that improves this one name can be hiding a defect in how we set the model up. Before adopting it, check it matches how that driver is built everywhere else.
drafts.evidence: Applied +0.012 at origin FY2024; average miss changed -0.012.
drafts.why_scope: If the correction turns out to be fixing our own mis-specification, the lesson is ALL and is about specification. If the company is genuinely unusual, it is STOCK.
drafts.overturned_by: Evidence that the driver is built the same way across the book and this name still needs the correction.
